---
title: "Countries, regions and currency"
jupyter: python3
---

```{python}
import pandas as pd

import ezrsurvey as ez
```

Two columns make a multi-country study harder than a single-market one. The
country question is usually free text, so it comes back holding every spelling a
person can produce. And if respondents answered about money in their own
currency, the amounts column cannot be averaged at all.

## The country column people typed

On one real open salary survey of 26,232 people, nine thousand wrote "United
States", eight thousand wrote "USA", two and a half thousand wrote "US", and
several hundred more wrote "U.S.", "Usa" or "usa". Matching on the name as typed
resolved about half the column.

`recode_region()` folds the answer down before looking it up. Case, punctuation,
accents and a leading "the" all stop mattering, and then a table of the
spellings people actually use is tried.

```{python}
ez.recode_region(["United States", "USA", "U.S.", "Estados Unidos"])
```

It carries the constituent countries of the United Kingdom, which a UK
respondent is as likely to write as the country itself:

```{python}
ez.recode_region(["England", "Scotland", "Wales", "Northern Ireland"])
```

Endonyms, because a survey fielded in more than one language collects them:

```{python}
ez.recode_region(["Deutschland", "Brasil", "Espana", "Osterreich"])
```

And the official ISO 3166-1 names, which is what a questionnaire built on the
standard puts in front of a respondent, in either word order:

```{python}
ez.recode_region(["Viet Nam", "Syrian Arab Republic", "Republic of Moldova", "Cabo Verde", "Eswatini"])
```

The fold is done letter by letter rather than left to the platform's
transliteration, so a name carrying an accent matches the same way on Windows,
macOS and Linux:

```{python}
ez.recode_region(["Côte d'Ivoire", "Réunion", "Türkiye"])
```

## Adding the column

`add_region()` does the same thing to a data frame, and `subregion=True` adds
the finer grouping alongside:

```{python}
survey = ez.add_region(ez.podracing_survey, "demo_country", subregion=True)

ez.calc_percentage(survey, "region", sort="desc")
```

```{python}
ez.calc_percentage(survey, "subregion", sort="desc")
```

Anything that did not match comes back missing with a warning naming the
values, because at that point what is left is genuine typos worth seeing rather
than spellings worth supporting.

## Reporting against the standard

A client who consolidates research across agencies wants countries coded to ISO
3166-1, not to whatever names this analyst happened to pick. A column already
coded that way needs no preparation:

```{python}
ez.recode_region(["US", "GBR", "DE", "JPN", "AUS"])
```

A two-letter code that is also an ordinary English word is only read as a
country when it was typed in capitals, so `"NO"` is Norway and `"no"` is
somebody answering a different question:

```{python}
ez.recode_region(["NO", "no"], quiet=True)
```

The bundled table carries both codes, so a country name can be replaced by its
code on the way out. That is the table to join to, because country names differ
between sources and codes do not:

```{python}
ez.country_region.head()
```

```{python}
codes = ez.country_region[["country", "iso2", "iso3"]]
coded = survey.merge(codes, left_on="demo_country", right_on="country", how="left")

coded.groupby(["iso3", "region"]).size().sort_values(ascending=False).head(8)
```

> Namibia's alpha-2 code is the two letters `NA`, not a missing value. It is
> worth knowing before filtering that column, and before reading a country file
> with pandas, which treats `"NA"` as missing unless told
> `keep_default_na=False`. The bundled table already keeps it.

The regions themselves follow the UN M49 sub-regions with two deliberate
departures, because they are how consumer research buys these markets: the
Middle East is a region of its own rather than part of Asia and Africa, and the
Americas are split north and south.

## Money in eleven currencies

A single amount converts with `convert_currency()`. The source currency is
`from_`, because `from` is a reserved word in Python:

```{python}
ez.convert_currency(50000, from_="GBP", to="USD")
```

```{python}
ez.convert_currency([50000, 60000], from_=["EUR", "CAD"], to="USD")
```

A whole column converts with `add_currency()`, which takes the currency from a
second column, so each row is converted at its own rate:

```{python}
pay = pd.DataFrame({
    "respondent": [1, 2, 3, 4, 5],
    "salary": [52000, 61000, 48000, 75000, 39000],
    "currency": ["GBP", "EUR", "USD", "CAD", "AUD"],
})

ez.add_currency(pay, "salary", from_="currency", to="EUR", into="salary_eur")
```

The rates are bundled rather than fetched, so a figure computed today is the
same figure next year. That is what a published number needs, and it is also why
they are a dated snapshot rather than live rates.

```{python}
ez.list_currencies()[:6]
```

When accuracy matters more than reproducibility, pass your own:

```{python}
own_rates = {"USD": 1, "GBP": 0.79, "EUR": 0.92}
ez.convert_currency(50000, from_="GBP", to="EUR", rates=own_rates)
```

A code the table does not hold is reported rather than guessed at. Real currency
columns contain things like `"AUD/NZD"` and `"Other"`, and those rows come back
missing with a warning naming the codes.
